**Research note: PostgreSQL identifier length, column limit, and default `max_connections`**

PostgreSQL identifiers, such as table, column, and constraint names, are limited to 63 bytes by default. The lexical-structure chapter explains that the server uses at most NAMEDATALEN-1 bytes of an identifier, that longer names are accepted but truncated, and that NAMEDATALEN defaults to 64 (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-syntax-lexical.html). The limits appendix gives the same figure as 63 bytes, and notes that it can be increased only by recompiling PostgreSQL (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). Because the limit is measured in bytes, multi-byte UTF-8 names will reach it in fewer characters than ASCII names.

A table can have up to 1,600 columns. The same limits appendix lists this as the maximum columns per table, and adds that the real ceiling can be lower because each row must fit within one 8 KB heap page (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/limits.html). For example, 1,600 `int` columns (about 6,400 bytes) fit, but 1,600 `bigint` columns (about 12,800 bytes) do not. Wide schemas should be checked against tuple size, not just the column count.

The default `max_connections` is typically 100. The connection-settings reference says the value may be lower if the kernel cannot support it, as determined during `initdb`. It also states that the setting can only be changed at server start, and that increasing it raises shared-memory allocation (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-connection.html). Superuser reserved connections come out of that total, so the pool's ceiling should be set below the server's limit.

**Recommendation:** Size the pool well below `max_connections`, and leave headroom for superuser, replication, and maintenance sessions. Keep identifiers under 63 bytes and check wide tables against the single-page tuple limit before the schema is finalized.

**Research note: default memory and WAL settings in PostgreSQL**

This note answers three questions about a fresh PostgreSQL install, using the current (PostgreSQL 18) official documentation.

**work_mem.** The default is 4 megabytes. This is the amount of memory each sort or hash operation can use before it spills to temporary disk files. A single query can run several such operations at once, and each session can run several queries, so the total memory use can be a multiple of this value. (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html)

**shared_buffers.** The documented default is typically 128 megabytes, but the server may pick a smaller value if the kernel will not support that allocation. The value is set during initdb, so a fresh install may not end up with exactly 128MB. (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html)

**max_wal_size.** The default is 1 GB. This is a soft target for how much write-ahead log can accumulate between automatic checkpoints. The server may exceed it under heavy write load, and a checkpoint is triggered when it is approached. (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html)

**Recommendation.** Leave work_mem at 4MB globally and raise it per session or per role for queries that need larger sorts, because the value is multiplied by the number of concurrent operations. Check the shared_buffers value the server actually reports after initdb before assuming 128MB, and consider raising max_wal_size on write-heavy systems to reduce checkpoint frequency.

```json
{"answers": {"1": "4MB", "2": "128MB (typically; may be lower if the kernel does not support it, set at initdb)", "3": "1GB"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html"], "2": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-resource.html"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-wal.html"]}}
```

**Research note: analytics side-store next to PostgreSQL (DuckDB or SQLite), and MERGE on PostgreSQL 15**

I checked three facts against primary pages, and each answer below comes from a page I read in this session.

**DuckDB memory.** DuckDB's default memory limit is 80% of physical RAM. The DuckDB team's memory-management article says the limit "is set to 80% of the physical RAM of your system" (source: https://duckdb.org/2024/07/09/memory-management.html). The article is from July 2024, and I did not confirm that the current documentation still says the same. The DuckDB out-of-memory guide redirected me without the value, so I could not check it there. Its advice to lower the limit when the OS kills the process still applies, because some operations reserve memory outside the buffer manager.

**SQLite file size.** The SQLite limits page gives a maximum database file size of 281 terabytes (source: https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html). That figure assumes the maximum page size of 65536 bytes and 4294967294 pages. With the default 4096-byte page size, the limit is about 17.5 TB. Older sources that still cite 140 TB are out of date. The filesystem will usually hit its own size limit first.

**PostgreSQL MERGE.** MERGE first appeared in PostgreSQL 15. The PostgreSQL 15 release notes list "Add SQL MERGE command to adjust one table to match another," described as similar to INSERT ... ON CONFLICT but more batch-oriented (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/release-15.html). If your colleague is on PostgreSQL 14 or earlier, MERGE is not available, and the upgrade is the only route to it. Upgrading to any 15.x minor release gives the same command.

**Recommendation.** If the side-store is for read-heavy analytical queries over data that fits on one machine, DuckDB is the better fit: its columnar engine and memory cap are designed for that workload, and its default limit is generous. SQLite suits small, embedded, or write-heavy workloads, and it has no analytics-oriented optimizer.

```json
{"answers": {"1": "80% of physical RAM", "2": "281 TB", "3": "15"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://duckdb.org/2024/07/09/memory-management.html"], "2": ["https://www.sqlite.org/limits.html"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/15/release-15.html"]}}
```

**Research note: TLS versions, host naming and HTTP status codes**

**TLS 1.3.** TLS 1.3 is specified by RFC 8446, "The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3", dated August 2018 (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446). That RFC is now obsolete. Its replacement, RFC 9846, carries the same title, is a Proposed Standard on the Internet Standards Track, and states that it obsoletes RFC 8446 (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9846). The guideline should cite RFC 9846 as the current specification and mention RFC 8446 as the version many existing references and implementations still use. I did not find a publication date on the RFC 9846 page, so I have not given one.

**Host name labels.** A single DNS label is limited to 63 octets. RFC 1035 states that "the remaining six bits of the length field limit the label to 63 octets or less" in section 3.1, and repeats the limit as "labels 63 octets or less" in section 2.3.4 (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035). The limit applies to each dot-separated component, not to the full name. The full name has its own separate limit, which this note does not cover.

**HTTP 418.** The status code 418 "I'm a teapot" is defined in RFC 2324, "Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol (HTCPCP/1.0)", in section 2.3.2. The definition reads: "Any attempt to brew coffee with a teapot should result in the error code "418 I'm a teapot"" (source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324). The code is a joke in the RFC itself and is not used for real errors, so the guideline should not rely on it for any actual HTTP behaviour. I did not check the RFC's status line or its later history, so I have not characterised either.

**Recommendation.** Cite RFC 9846 rather than RFC 8446 for TLS 1.3 in the guideline, and state the 63-octet per-label limit from RFC 1035 wherever host naming rules appear. Leave 418 out of any production status-code table, and note that it appears only in the joke RFC.

{"answers": {"1": "RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3); superseded by RFC 9846", "2": "63 octets", "3": "418 I'm a teapot, defined in RFC 2324"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446", "https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9846"], "2": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035"], "3": ["https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2324"]}}

**Research note: timeouts, grace periods and Docker networking for the deploy runbook**

**Lambda timeout.** A standard Lambda function's timeout can be set up to 900 seconds (15 minutes); the default is 3 seconds, set in 1-second steps (source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html). The same page notes one exception: functions on AWS Lambda Managed Instances, for asynchronous and event source mapping invocations (except Amazon MQ and Amazon DocumentDB), allow up to 5,400 seconds (source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html). The runbook should state 900 seconds as the ceiling for ordinary functions, because a long job that needs more than 15 minutes will be killed mid-run.

**Kubernetes grace period.** A Pod's default terminationGracePeriodSeconds is 30 seconds. The Pod lifecycle page says "The default `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` setting is 30 seconds" (source: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/). The value is a Pod-spec field, so the runbook should note that any service needing longer shutdown must set it explicitly, and that a `kubectl delete --grace-period` flag can override it per deletion.

**Docker default bridge subnet.** Docker's network overview says that when no `--subnet` is given, Docker picks from predefined default address pools, and the first built-in entry is `172.17.0.0/16` (source: https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/). That is the subnet Docker's default bridge uses for containers. I could not confirm from a page I read that docker0 itself is fixed to this range. The dockerd reference only says docker0 is the default bridge and gives no address (source: https://docs.docker.com/engine/reference/commandline/dockerd). Treat 172.17.0.0/16 as the answer, but check `ip addr show docker0` on the target host. The pool can be changed in `/etc/docker/daemon.json`, which matters if the local subnet clashes with a corporate network.

**Recommendation.** Put the three values in the runbook as "Lambda: 900 s max; Kubernetes: 30 s default grace period, set per Pod if longer; local Docker: 172.17.0.0/16 by default," with the sources linked for future readers. Add a note that the local Docker value should be verified on each developer machine, since the address pool is configurable.

{"answers": {"1": "900 seconds (15 minutes)", "2": "30 seconds", "3": "172.17.0.0/16"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-timeout.html"], "2": ["https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/"], "3": ["https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/"]}}

**Research note: test and tooling defaults**

**Vitest per-test timeout.** Vitest's default `testTimeout` is 5,000 ms in Node.js, and it rises to 15,000 ms when `browser.enabled` is true (source: https://vitest.dev/config/testtimeout). A value of 0 disables the timeout, and the CLI flag `--testTimeout=<ms>` overrides it per run.

**Linux kernel with Rust.** Initial Rust support first landed in mainline with Linux 6.1, which was released on 11 December 2022 (source: https://lwn.net/Articles/910762/). The merge was deliberately minimal: it covered building loadable modules and a small sample module, with no drivers (source: https://www.debugpoint.com/linux-kernel-6-1/). Rust support is optional at build time. LWN also noted that no production 6.1 system would run Rust code, so the team should treat 6.1 as the start of the infrastructure rather than a usable Rust driver base.

**PostgreSQL statement_timeout.** The default is 0, which disables the timeout (source: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html). The docs state that "a value of zero (the default) disables the timeout." A mirror of the reference lists the same default as "0 (0ms)" (source: https://postgresqlco.nf/en/doc/param/statement_timeout). The official page is the authority for this value.

**Recommendation.** Keep Vitest's 5-second default for unit tests and raise it only for specific slow suites, since 15 seconds applies only in browser mode. Leave `statement_timeout` at 0 in the server config and set a non-zero value per role or per session in the application's test and worker connections, so a runaway query fails fast without affecting every session.

```json
{"answers": {"1": "5000 ms in Node.js (15000 ms when browser mode is enabled)", "2": "6.1", "3": "0 (disabled)"}, "sources": {"1": ["https://vitest.dev/config/testtimeout"], "2": ["https://lwn.net/Articles/910762/", "https://www.debugpoint.com/linux-kernel-6-1/"], "3": ["https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html", "https://postgresqlco.nf/en/doc/param/statement_timeout"]}}
```
